title: Search, Enclosed
author: Andrew Cantarutti
summary: Andrew Cantarutti reads Google's announcement that schools declining its AI will lose access to Google Search as a modern act of enclosure. He compares the decision to the English enclosure acts that turned common land into private property, arguing that the real issue was always who gets to decide. He documents how deeply Google products saturate schools, quotes internal documents describing a pipeline of future users, and notes the concentration risks seen in the Microsoft outage and the PowerSchool breach. On evidence, he points to the Penn study of Turkish high school math students and to Common Sense Media testing to argue that nothing yet justifies making AI the price of search. His practical response is to treat the ultimatum as a lesson plan: teach enclosure and monopoly, have students compare Google's AI overviews with AI-free search engines, change default search engines on Chromebooks, write exit and data-portability terms into vendor contracts, and bargain collectively.
points: Google's position is that schools may set any AI policy they like so long as it keeps search on, which makes the vendor, not the school, the real policy authority.
The enclosure analogy shifts the question from productivity to governance: schools lost a customary expectation of open search rather than a piece of property.
Leaked litigation documents describe school products as a pipeline of future users, undercutting the claim that educational efficacy drives the product.
The best available evidence shows the best case for guardrailed AI tutoring is no harm done, so evidence does not justify tying AI to search.
Concrete steps are to change default search engines, include exit and data-portability terms in contracts, bargain as consortia, and use the ultimatum as a classroom case study.
quotes: Phillips and his team at Google made the decision, but they’ve left schools to deliver the bad news. It’s a perfect picture of the bargain we struck when we asked the private sector to supply our digital infrastructure.
Strip away the language of “control” and “choice”, and what’s left is simple. Schools can set whatever AI policy they like, so long as Google approves of it.
Economic historians are right that enclosure made English agriculture more productive. But that’s a reduction of the larger argument. The argument was about who got to decide.
One presentation described it as building a “pipeline of future users.” Another stated, “You get that loyalty early, and potentially for life.
Regardless of where the case ends up, the lesson for schools remains the same. Our AI policies are only as sovereign as the vendor allows.
In other words, the best-case scenario wasn’t better performance; it was no harm done.
The Walled Garden has never said “never.” It says “not before there’s evidence.” But a school that wants to see the evidence first must now give up search in the meantime.
As I’ve written before, the relationship between a company and its market is transactional while the relationship between a school and its students is fiduciary.
Changing the default search engine on students’ Chromebooks is cheap, it’s reversible, and it can be done before Google’s new rules take effect.
